name: Send and receive basic Morse code
blurb: Beyond recognising letters: actually holding a conversation. Sending is easier than receiving, and good sending rhythm is what makes you readable.
gear: A straight key or a paddle, plus a practice oscillator
steps: Get receiving to about 10 words per minute first. Sending well requires knowing what good code sounds like.
Learn to send with a straight key: correct wrist action, and the timing ratios — a dash is three dots, gaps between elements one dot, between letters three, between words seven.
Record your sending and compare it to machine-generated code. Bad rhythm is far harder for a receiver than high speed.
Learn the procedural signals and common abbreviations that make real exchanges efficient.
Practise head copy — understanding without writing down — which is the step to conversational speed.
Make real contacts, on air with a licence or over an internet Morse practice server.
tips: Rhythm matters more than speed. Sloppy timing is unreadable at any speed.
Getting on the air requires an amateur radio licence in most countries. Practice servers do not.
proof: You hold a short two-way exchange at 12 words per minute, sending and receiving.
